A subsidy is money given — usually by a government — to a person, a business, or an industry to help them financially, so that they can either survive, grow, or offer their goods and services at a lower price than they otherwise could.

Think of it this way: imagine you sell apples, but growing them costs you $2 per apple. If you sell each apple for $2, you break even. If you sell for less, you lose money. Now the government steps in and gives you $0.50 per apple to help cover your costs. You can now afford to sell apples for $1.50 instead of $2. The customer pays less. You don't lose money. The government made this possible by bridging the gap. That bridge is a subsidy.

In short, a subsidy is a financial push from a powerful entity (almost always a government) that makes something cheaper, easier, or more viable than the free market alone would allow.
What a Subsidy Actually Does

A subsidy reduces the cost burden on whoever receives it. That burden doesn't disappear — it just shifts. Instead of the buyer or the producer bearing the full cost, the government (and by extension, the taxpaying public) absorbs a portion of it. This is the essential mechanic: a subsidy is a transfer of financial responsibility from one party to another.
Who Gives Subsidies?

The giver is almost always a government — local, national, or international bodies. Occasionally, large organizations or institutions also provide subsidies (for example, a university might subsidize a student's meals), but when you encounter this word in everyday life — in newspapers, economics classes, or political debates — it almost always refers to government money.
Who Receives Subsidies?

Subsidies can be directed at many different recipients.

Businesses and industries are very common recipients. Governments may subsidize farmers so that food stays affordable, or subsidize airlines to keep remote regions connected, or subsidize steel manufacturers to protect domestic jobs.

Individual people can also receive subsidies. When a government helps low-income families pay their rent, or covers part of a person's health insurance premium, or makes public transport tickets cheaper than their real cost, those are subsidies directed at individuals.

Other countries can receive subsidies too, though this usually happens under the umbrella of foreign aid or international development programs.
Why Do Governments Give Subsidies?

This is the heart of understanding the word, because the reason behind a subsidy tells you a lot about its nature.

To make essential goods affordable. Food, medicine, energy, and housing are things people cannot go without. If the free market prices these too high for ordinary people, governments may subsidize producers or sellers to bring prices down.

To support struggling industries. If an important industry is going through a hard time — say, falling global prices are threatening domestic farmers — a government might offer subsidies to keep those farmers in business until conditions improve.

To encourage desirable behavior. Governments use subsidies as a nudge. If a government wants more people to buy electric cars (because they're better for the environment), it might subsidize electric vehicles to make them cheaper and more attractive. If it wants more solar panels installed, it subsidizes solar energy. The subsidy acts as an incentive, steering both businesses and consumers toward choices the government considers beneficial.

To protect national security interests. Some industries — defense, food production, energy — are considered too strategically important to let fail. Governments may subsidize them even when they're not economically efficient, simply to ensure the country remains self-sufficient.

To compete internationally. If another country is subsidizing its own steel industry, its steel becomes artificially cheap on the global market. A competing country might subsidize its own steel industry just to keep its manufacturers from being priced out.
What Forms Can a Subsidy Take?

A subsidy doesn't always mean handing someone a bag of cash. It can come in several forms.

Direct cash payments are the most straightforward — the government literally sends money to the recipient. A farmer receiving a payment per ton of wheat produced is getting a direct subsidy.

Tax reductions or exemptions are extremely common. If the government says "businesses that invest in renewable energy will pay less tax," the reduced tax bill is effectively a subsidy — the government is giving up money it would have collected, and that sacrifice benefits the recipient.

Low-interest loans are another form. If the government lends money to a struggling business at an interest rate far below what a bank would charge, the difference in interest is a hidden subsidy.

Price controls combined with compensation also count. A government might force a utility company to charge low electricity prices (benefiting consumers), but then compensate the utility company for its losses. The compensation is the subsidy.
A Few Concrete, Real-World Examples

Agricultural subsidies are among the most widespread in the world. In many countries, governments pay farmers directly or guarantee minimum prices for crops. Without this support, small-scale farming might be economically unviable against cheap imports.

Energy subsidies include government support for fossil fuels (making petrol or gas cheaper at the pump) as well as support for renewable energy (making solar panels or wind turbines more affordable to install).

Housing subsidies appear when governments help low-income people afford rent — through direct housing vouchers or by funding the construction of affordable housing.

Education subsidies happen when a government funds public schools or universities so that students pay tuition far below the actual cost of running those institutions. The government covers the gap.

Healthcare subsidies occur when a government pays part of citizens' medical costs or insurance premiums, ensuring that healthcare is accessible even to those who couldn't afford it at market rates.
The Debate Around Subsidies

Subsidies are not neutral. They are one of the most contested tools in economics and politics, and understanding that debate is part of truly knowing the word.

The case for subsidies rests on the idea that markets, left entirely alone, sometimes produce bad outcomes for society. They may price essential goods out of reach for poor people, they may let important industries collapse, or they may ignore the long-term benefits of things like clean energy that the market undervalues. Subsidies are seen as a correction — a way for society to steer the economy toward outcomes it values.

The case against subsidies argues that they distort the natural workings of supply and demand. When a government artificially props up an industry, it may be keeping an inefficient or outdated industry alive at taxpayers' expense. Subsidies can also create unfair competition — businesses that don't receive subsidies struggle to compete against those that do. Critics also argue that subsidized industries can become dependent and never learn to stand on their own.

There is also the question of who ultimately benefits. A subsidy meant to lower prices for consumers might, in practice, end up increasing profits for producers instead — if producers simply raise their own prices knowing the government is covering part of the cost. This is a well-known problem economists study carefully.
Subsidy vs. Some Words It's Often Confused With

Subsidy vs. grant: A grant is also money given (often without needing to be repaid), but grants are usually for specific, one-time projects — like funding a research study or building a community center. A subsidy is more of an ongoing financial support tied to production, behavior, or consumption over time.

Subsidy vs. loan: A loan must be repaid. A subsidy does not. If the government lends you money, that's a loan. If it gives you money or reduces your costs with no repayment required, that's a subsidy (though as mentioned, low-interest loans can function as a partial subsidy).

Subsidy vs. tax: A tax takes money away from people or businesses and gives it to the government. A subsidy moves in the opposite direction — it gives money from the government to people or businesses. Some economists actually describe subsidies as "negative taxes" for this reason.
The Plural
The plural form is subsidies. "The government announced new subsidies for electric vehicle manufacturers." "Agricultural subsidies have been controversial for decades."
Putting It All Together

A subsidy is a financial lifeline or advantage given — almost always by a government — to reduce costs, encourage certain actions, or protect something deemed important to society. It shifts part of the financial burden away from producers or consumers and onto the government (and therefore taxpayers). It is a powerful economic tool that can do enormous good when well-designed, and considerable harm when misused or misdirected. Understanding subsidies means understanding one of the most fundamental ways governments shape economies and daily life.
